001.title: Chest Pain
001.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 16:00 Temperature: 37.0 C (98.6 degrees F) Pulse: 120 beats/min, Weak Respiratory rate: 34 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 100 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 60 mm Hg Height: 183cm (72.0 in) Weight: 97.5 kg (215 lb) Body Mass Index: 29.1 kg/m2
exam: Tachycardic, regular rhythm, no new murmur
001.clinical_tip: Needle decompression before CXR in the unstable patient — do not delay treatment for imaging.
001.objective: Immediate decompression and chest tube; 100% oxygen.

interventions.label: Move to Emergency Department
interventions.why: Acute respiratory failure requires ED care.

interventions.label: 100% Oxygen
interventions.why: Maximize oxygenation while preparing decompression.

interventions.label: Pulse ox + cardiac monitor
interventions.why: Track oxygenation and hemodynamics continuously.

interventions.label: IV access
interventions.why: Large-bore access if hypotensive or peri-arrest.

interventions.label: Needle decompression
interventions.why: Clinical diagnosis — treat before imaging if unstable.

interventions.label: Tube thoracostomy
interventions.why: Definitive management after needle decompression.

interventions.label: Chest X-ray
interventions.why: Confirm tube placement after stabilization.

decoys.label: Administer a sedative
decoys.why: Sedatives are not typically administered initially in tension pneumothorax as they can worsen respiratory depression

decoys.label: Start antibiotics
decoys.why: Antibiotics are not necessary for a primary diagnosis of tension pneumothorax unless there is a secondary infection present

decoys.label: Apply a hot pack to the affected area
decoys.why: Heat application is not beneficial in cases of tension pneumothorax as it can increase intrathoracic pressure and worsen symptoms

decoys.label: Prescribe a blood transfusion
decoys.why: A blood transfusion would not be appropriate for a primary diagnosis of tension pneumothorax unless there is severe anemia or hemorrhage present

easy.intro: Initial History Reason(s) for visit: Chest pain; respiratory distress History of present Illness: The patient, a 65-year-old accountant, is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from the trucking company, where he works. Ten minutes prior to the ambulance’s arrival, the patient developed excruciating, sharp pain on the right side of his chest accompanied by marked respiratory distress. He rates the pain as an 8 on a 10-point scale. The pain increases on respiration, and he is unable to answer questions. A coworker who accompanied the patient to the hospital says that this has never happened to the patient in the past. Coworker mentions patient has a past medical history of emphysema and asthma. Oxygen was administered during transport.

002.title: Altered Mental Status
002.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 11:00 Temperature: 36.8 C (98.2 degrees F) Pulse: 88 beats/min. Regular rhythm Respiratory rate: 18 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 115 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 85 mm Hg Height: 180cm (70.9 in) Weight: 91.0 kg (200.6 lb) Body Mass Index: 27.9 kg/m2
exam: Confused, follows simple commands; gait unsteady after recent fall
002.clinical_tip: Elderly or alcoholic with AMS after minor trauma — non-contrast CT head first.
002.objective: Identify bleed, reverse coagulopathy, neurosurgical evacuation if indicated.

interventions.label: Emergency Department
interventions.why: Acute neurologic change needs ED evaluation.

interventions.label: Seizure precautions
interventions.why: Prevent secondary brain injury from seizures.

interventions.label: Non-contrast CT head
interventions.why: Crescent-shaped subdural collection.

interventions.label: PT/INR and platelets
interventions.why: Identify coagulopathy before neurosurgery.

interventions.label: CBC
interventions.why: Baseline and transfusion planning.

interventions.label: Neurosurgery consult
interventions.why: Evacuation if midline shift or decline.

interventions.label: Neurologic checks + monitor
interventions.why: Detect herniation early.

decoys.label: Admit the patient to a general ward
decoys.why: Subdural hematoma is an emergency and requires immediate attention. Admission to a general ward might not provide the necessary level of care, monitoring, or resources for such a critical condition.

decoys.label: Prescribe pain medication but without any CT scan
decoys.why: Pain management is important, but it should be done after confirming the cause of the head injury. Without a CT scan, the cause cannot be accurately identified, and the wrong treatment might be prescribed.

decoys.label: Administer a blood thinner to prevent further clotting
decoys.why: Subdural hematoma is caused by bleeding between the brain and skull. Administering a blood thinner could potentially worsen the condition by accelerating the bleeding.

decoys.label: Start the patient on antiepileptic drugs for seizure prophylaxis without a history of seizures
decoys.why: Antiepileptic drugs are used to prevent seizures, but they should only be administered if the patient has a history of seizures or if seizures have occurred during the initial evaluation. In the absence of these factors, their use is unnecessary and potentially harmful.

easy.intro: Initial History Reason(s) for visit: Altered mental status History of present Illness: A 70-year-old Caucasian man comes to the Emergency room because his family members are concerned that something is wrong. The patient has been having behavioral changes over a period of three or four weeks. He used to be very active and managed all of his financial affairs. He now barely talks, stares at the wall for hours at a time, and sleeps most of the day. Four weeks ago, the patient got up to urinate and fell before reaching the bathroom. He was found on the floor the next morning by family members. He was taken to his family doctor and was discharged with a prescription to buy a cane. Since that time, he has been having problems walking. There have been no fevers or night sweats. The patient is currently in no pain. Past Medical History: Chronic alcohol abuse; cataracts. Hospitalization Procedures: Hemorrhoidectomy 1 year ago. Last colonoscopy was 4 years ago which demonstrated no abnormalities. Current medications: Aspirin 81mg PO daily Allergies: None Vaccinations: Up to date Family History: Father: Deceased due to a 'heart attack'. Mother: Diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus and died of natural causes. The patient has no siblings. Social History: Marital/Family: Widowed; he has three children. Personal habits: the patient smokes 1 Pack/day. He currently does not drink alcohol but was a chronic alcoholic for 30 years. Denies use of illegal drugs or misuse of medications. Occupation/educational: He is a retired Army human resources manager. He is a high school graduate. Recreational: The patient likes to spend time with his children and enjoys collecting stamps. standard.hpi:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Altered mental status
History of present Illness:
A 70-year-old Caucasian man comes to the Emergency room because his family members are concerned that something is wrong. The patient has been having behavioral changes over a period of three or four weeks. He used to be very active and managed all of his financial affairs. He now barely talks, stares at the wall for hours at a time, and sleeps most of the day. Four weeks ago, the patient got up to urinate and fell before reaching the bathroom. He was found on the floor the next morning by family members. He was taken to his family doctor and was discharged with a prescription to buy a cane. Since that time, he has been having problems walking. There have been no fevers or night sweats. The patient is currently in no pain. 

Past Medical History: Chronic alcohol abuse; cataracts.

Hospitalization Procedures: Hemorrhoidectomy 1 year ago. Last colonoscopy was 4 years ago which demonstrated no abnormalities.

Current medications: Aspirin 81mg PO daily

Allergies: None

Vaccinations: Up to date

Family History:
Father: Deceased due to a 'heart attack'.
Mother: Diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus and died of natural causes. 
The patient has no siblings.

Social History: Marital/Family: Widowed; he has three children. Personal habits: the patient smokes 1 Pack/day. He currently does not drink alcohol but was a chronic alcoholic for 30 years. Denies use of illegal drugs or misuse of medications.

Occupation/educational: He is a retired Army human resources manager. He is a high school graduate.

Recreational: The patient likes to spend time with his children and enjoys collecting stamps.

Review of systems:
General: See HPI
Skin: Negative
HEENT: Negative
Cardiorespiratory: Negative
Gastrointestinal: Negative
Genitourinary: Negative
Neuropsychiatric: See HPI

121.title: Poor Feeding
121.diagnosis: Failure to Thrive (FTT) or Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) are common considerations for Poor Feeding of unknown cause in pediatric patients.
exam: Poor Feeding — exam tailored to chief complaint on arrival.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
121.clinical_tip: Febrile infant — sepsis workup, fluids, and close monitoring before disposition.
